   INTERVENOR GEORGE NOELKE’S NOTICE OF LEGISLATIVE TESTIMONY

COMES NOW, George Noelke (“Noelke”), pro se Intervenor in CCN 59182 and 59475 appearing
conditionally and solely to provide notice of his public testimony at the Senate Business and Commerce
Committee hearing on July 29, 2026.

    A.​ The Senate Business and Commerce Committee
            1.​ Interim Charge: On March 27, 2026, The Texas Lt. Governor, Dan Patrick, issued the
                following interim charge to the Senate Business and Commerce Committee: ​
                Managing the Impacts of 765-kv Transmission Lines on Private Property Rights:
            Review the proposed 765-kv transmission line route plans to determine their impact on
           homes, businesses, and communities. Assess whether the current regulatory processes
           and timelines are sufficient in protecting landowner rights, including allowing for proper
           consideration of the effect of high voltage transmission lines on long-term land use,
           property values, and environmental factors. Recommend ways to improve transmission
           planning, permitting, and siting decisions for the infrastructure necessary to serve growth
           in the state. ​


       2.​ The Committee Hearing: The Senate Business and Commerce Committee held a public
           hearing on July 29, 2026 to take testimony from landowners on this charge. Noelke, as
           well as many other landowners, attended and spoke at this hearing. Noelke also
           submitted written testimony to the Committee. ​


       3.​ Committee Chairman Schwertner’s Statements after the Hearing. Two days after the
           hearing, on July 31, 2026, Chairman Schwertner released a public statement that he
           would be, “calling on the PUC to deny the existing CCN applications. Any
           reapplications need to take into consideration the concerns raised during our hearing. The
           Legislature will reform the CCN process next session to ensure future projects are fair
           and transparent.” See Attachment A for his complete statement.​


B.​ Noelke’s Testimony: In recognition and support of Chairman Schwertner’s statement, Noelke
   attaches his written testimony that he submitted to the Committee at the hearing. See Attachmnt B
   for his complete statement. His spoken testimony to the Committee was an abbreviated version of
   this statement since the Committee’s rules allowed for only two minutes to speak.​


C.​ Response by PUC: The PUC response to Chairman Schwertner is not favorable. Within five
   hours of Chairman Schwertner’s statement, the Commission Counsel, Ron Olson, filed on the
   Interchange in 59182 a memo to the ALJ’s advising them that the deadline for their response to
   the PFD exceptions and replies is August 17, 2026. See Item 569. He reiterated that the PFD
   “will be considered by the commissioners at a future open meeting.” In other words, the PUC is
   barrelling towards a final agency decision in 59182 with a PFD that the Commission already
   knows is favored by the Applicants (see Applicants’ late filed exceptions to the PFD at Item
   565), notwithstanding Chairman Schwertner’s recommendation that all CCN applications be




                                                                                                     2
         denied.​


    D.​ Noelke’s Response: ​
        1. PUC Chairman Thomas Gleeson testified to the Senate Business and Commerce Committee on
        July 29, 2026 that none of the 765 kV CCN applications have been finalized with a final agency
        order. This is an essential procedural fact under the Texas APA, Texas Gov’t Code Chapter 2001.
        Among other things, this means the administrative remedies have not yet been exhausted and that
        the PUC staff still has the discretion to withdraw its referral of the 765 kV cases to SOAH. ​
        2. Noelke observes that Mr. Olson’s July 31, 2026 memo (See Item 569) setting the August 17,
        2026 deadline for the ALJ’s is no different than his previous memo dated July 16, 2026 (Item
        555) setting the date for the exceptions and replies. Mr. Olson’s deadlines all come after the July
        14, 2026 cutoff date. And, he has again failed to state how he was operating under color of law
        considering the passing of the 180 day deadline on July 14, 2026. Consistent with his prior
        arguments (see Item 554), Noelke observes that a) Mr. Olson’s directive to SOAH setting the
        August 17, 2026 deadline is an ultra vires act, b) the ALJ’s response to that deadline will be an
        ultra vires act, and c) the Commissioners receiving oral argument and otherwise considering the
        merits of the PFD by entering a final agency order will be an ultra vires act. Regardless of
        whether the Commission intends to follow Chairman Schwertner’s request to deny the CCN,
        all that the Commission can do lawfully in 59182 is the Commission staff can send a letter to
        SOAH withdrawing its referral. CCN 59182 was denied by operation of law on July 14, 2026.
        Like SOAH, the PUC’s only course of action now is simply to close the case. ​
        3. All of the 765 kV applications are in the exact same procedural posture; none have a final
        agency order entered by the PUC Commissioners. As such, all that is necessary to deny the CCN
        applications is a letter from PUC staff to SOAH withdrawing the referral.​


    E.​ Conditions: Intervenor Noelke files this notice conditionally, without waiving his earlier stated
        position that subject-matter jurisdiction over 59182 terminated by operation of law on July 14,
        2026. (See Items 554 and 566.)

Conclusion​
This filing is Noelke’s notice to all parties of his legislative testimony in light of Chairman Schwertner’s
statements. Noelke can only guess at the PUC’ s questionable motivations for continuing to seek a final
agency order in 59182, while ignoring Chairman Schwertner’s recommendations. Regardless, what is
certain (judging from outrage of the landowners who attended the July 29, 2026 legislative hearing) is



                                                                                                               3
 that the PUC’s resistance to addressing the obvious injustices raised in the Senate Business and
Commerce Committee further exposes this process as transparently unfair and weighted heavily for the
Applicants. The Commission is clearly missing the point by pursuing a final agency order in 59182 under
these circumstances. The open meeting (yet to be scheduled) to rule on the final agency order will
necessarily involve oral argument before the Commissioners by 59182 landowners, many of whom
testified at the July 29, 2026 Senate hearing. This will add insult to injury (plus added financial costs) for
those landowners, and such duplicative testimony will only further justify the need for legislative reform.​
​
Noelke is not seeking any relief relating to this notice. He further acknowledges that his legislative
testimony is not evidence in either 59182 or 59475.​
​
Dated: August 2, 2026

Respectfully submitted,​
​
​
/s/ George Noelke​
George Noelke​
Intervenor​
Pro se Landowner

 Attachment A

                       Statement from Chairman Charles Schwertner

AUSTIN, TX -- This week, the Senate Business and Commerce Committee held a 15-hour hearing to
examine the state of Texas' electricity market and the proposed 765kV ultra-high voltage transmission
lines intended to support load growth in West Texas

Testimony from property owners and their representatives highlighted significant concerns regarding the
certificate of convenience and necessity process (CCN), including the lack of proper notice from utilities,
shortened timelines for Public Utility Commission (PUC) proceedings, and due process at the State Office
of Administrative Hearings. These concerns demonstrate the need for a complete overhaul of the CCN
process before these applications can advance.

Accordingly, I am calling on the PUC to deny the existing CCN applications. Any reapplications need to
take into consideration the concerns raised during our hearing. The Legislature will reform the CCN
process next session to ensure future projects are fair and transparent.

(Posted on his X account on July 31 at 10:30 a.m.)

 Attachment B

                           Written Testimony of George Noelke​
                          Senate Business & Commerce Hearing
                          Regarding 765 kV Transmission Lines​
                                      July 29, 2026

Mr. Chairman and Members, thank you for giving me this opportunity to speak and submit
written testimony. My name is George Noelke, and I am a landowner in Irion County. I am also
an intervenor in CCN 59182 and 59475. ​

I am a licensed attorney, and I am pro se in these cases. I retired from the Texas Office of the
Attorney General in 2014 after 24 years as an Assistant Attorney General. For about half of that
time I served in the Administrative Law Division, where I provided general counsel services to
several state agencies, including the State Office of Administrative Hearings (SOAH). I also
defended agencies at District Court and above in contested case appeals under the Administrative
Procedure Act, Chapter 2001 of the Texas Government Code. The PUC was not one of my client
agencies, though I am familiar with this administrative process because of my appellate
experience.

I have three points I would like to make today.

First, I want to alert you to the Applicants’ lack of experience in a critical area. They have no
direct experience with managing a 765 kV line over two high pressured natural gas pipelines, the
Eiger and the Matterhorn. These pipelines will carry a combined 6.2 billion cubic feet of gas per
day by the time Applicants’ line is operational. This is a public safety issue not just where the
line and pipeline will cross, but anywhere along the pipeline corridor where AC interference
might interact with a pipeline anomaly. Matterhorn’s agents have been on my property for the
last two weeks addressing a pipeline anomaly.

Second, like other intervenors, I ask that you re-evaluate the State’s energy policy. My property,
as does many others where the Applicants’ proposed line intersects the Eiger and Matterhorn
pipelines, highlights the hypocrisy of giving the right of eminent domain to pipeline and electric
companies. These private and quasi governmental companies are profiting from taking energy
out of the Permian Basin and simultaneously transferring energy into the Permian Basin. The
losers are not only Texas landowners like myself who lose their land to eminent domain, but
electric consumers. Please note that Conclusion of Law # 16 in 59182 provides, “The CCN
amendments approved by this Order will not result in the probable lowering of costs to
consumers in the area. PURA § 37.056(c)(4)(E).” (Emphasis added. See Item 537 at page 156.)




                                                                                                 6
 And, third, I ask that you consider the 839 intervenors who were dismissed en masse for not
filing a position statement or direct testimony in 59475. These landowners were not afforded the
notice protections existing in the rules. I have several pleadings filed in 59475 making this point,
and my intention has been to create the foundation for an appeal. More than half of the
intervenor class in 59475 was severed by the Applicants before the hearing on the merits even
started. This without question is one of the greatest injustices caused by the aggressive 180 day
requirement in HB 5066. The Applicants, in a rush to beat a legislatively mandated clock, were
motivated to trim the number of Intervenors so that the case could reach the PUC within the180
days. The Applicants used nothing less than procedural trickery to cut their opponents off by
more than half. Above all, this case should be a stimulus for the legislature to limit the power of
eminent domain. In private hands, particularly here where there are tens if not hundreds of
billions of dollars at stake, that power is wielded for profits, not for the benefit of the people.

Finally, my position is that each of the 765 kV applications should be dismissed. I have filed my
Notice of Applicants’ Denial of CCN by Operation of Law in 59182 and ask for your review.
(See Item 554.) Now that 59182 has been denied by operation of law, each of the remaining
applications should be dismissed by the PUC because all were justified as necessary by the
Applicants based on their interpretation of the Permian Basin Reliability Plan. ​
​
This testimony, my pleadings and other relevant information can be found on my website at
http://www.governmentinthesun.com/765-kv-documents.

Thank you for your consideration today.
​
George Noelke​
Intervenor​
gnoelke@gmail.com
